title: Selective Self-Reference for LLM-as-a-Judge: Using Self-Consistency to Reduce Error Propagation

contributions.purpose: Identify that incorrect self-generated answers used as references degrade LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy on uncertain items.
contributions.mechanism: Analysis of always-reference judging on items with low agreement across sampled self-answers.
contributions.evaluation: On low-agreement items, always-reference achieves only 24.50% accuracy versus 37.75% for no-reference judging; unanimous five-sample agreement yields 78.66% self-answer correctness versus 35.51% at three-of-five.
contributions.source_quote: First, we identify the error propagation problem in self-reference judging, demonstrating that incorrect self-answers significantly degrade judgment accuracy on uncertain items.

contributions.purpose: Avoid error propagation while retaining the benefits of self-reference in judging.
contributions.mechanism: SSR-Judge samples multiple independent solutions via temperature sampling and applies an agreement-threshold gate to conditionally enable self-reference only under high self-consistency.
contributions.evaluation: Validated on MMLU-Pro pairwise preference judgment against no-reference and always-reference baselines.
contributions.source_quote: Second, we propose SSR-Judge, a selective self-reference method that uses self-consistency as a confidence gate to conditionally enable self-reference.

contributions.purpose: Demonstrate that confidence-gated self-reference outperforms both fixed strategies.
contributions.mechanism: Pairwise preference accuracy comparison on MMLU-Pro.
contributions.evaluation: SSR-Judge achieves 58.93% preference accuracy, outperforming no-reference (52.07%) and always self-reference (58.21%) baselines.
contributions.source_quote: Third, we demonstrate that SSR-Judge achieves 58.93% preference accuracy on MMLU-Pro, outperforming both no-reference (52.07%) and always self-reference (58.21%) baselines.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Lin et al. (2025) introduced self-reference-guided evaluation... While this improves accuracy when the self-answer is correct, they note the risk of error propagation when the self-answer is wrong... Our work connects these threads by using self-consistency to decide when self-reference should be applied in judging.
Our work addresses a complementary failure mode: error propagation from incorrect self-references, which we mitigate through confidence-gated self-reference.
Building on this insight, we propose Selective Self-Reference (SSR-Judge), a method that uses self-consistency to gate the use of self-reference in LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation.

notes: Near-tie result: headline gain over always self-reference is only 0.72pp (58.93% vs 58.21%); the clear gain is over no-reference (52.07%). Contributions given as inline prose list ('This work makes three contributions. First... Second... Third...'), not bullets.
